info.title: Hanzo Cloud API
info.description: Package todo is Hanzo Todo: boards, the work items on them, and the filters that make a board.

get.summary: Returns a board's issues — work items with their column, priority, assignee, labels and schedule.
get.description:
Returns a board's issues — work items with their column, priority,
assignee, labels and schedule.

WHICH board is a filter, not an address. Bound to a repository (the key from
the path) it is that project's board; left unbound it is the org's whole
board; narrowed by label it is a board smaller than any repository — which is
the only way an app that lives as a directory inside a shared repository can
have one. Every combination is the same rows through the same projection, so
no two boards can disagree about what a column means.

The column is a LABEL on the forge, so the board and the forge web UI are the
same object seen twice: relabelling in either moves the card in both. A closed
issue reads as done whatever its labels say.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description:
Key is the project whose issues to list, from the path. EMPTY means every
project in the org — the global board. It is a filter like the rest of
this struct rather than an address, which is what lets one op answer both
"this board" and "all the work" without a second surface disagreeing with
the first about what a column is.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description:
Status keeps only issues in that board column: backlog, todo, in_progress,
done or canceled. An unknown value is refused with 400.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description:
Kind keeps only work items of that shape: issue, pr or epic. An unknown
value is refused with 400.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description: Repo keeps only issues bound to that git repository.

parameters.name: label
parameters.description:
Label keeps only issues carrying that label, compared case-insensitively.

This is how a board narrows to something SMALLER than a repository — the
one mechanism for it. An estate whose apps are directories inside one
repository (hanzoai/cloud carries ~140 of them) has no repository per app
to address, so the app is a label: `label=app/meet` is the meet board.
Nothing is provisioned to make one exist; a board is the query.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description:
Source keeps only issues opened from that surface: team, git, crm,
helpdesk, cms or agent. An unknown value is refused with 400.

parameters.name: scheduled
parameters.description:
Scheduled keeps only issues that carry a date — a start, a due date or
both. This is the timeline's slice of the board: pass scheduled=true to
get exactly the rows a gantt has somewhere to draw, instead of fetching
every issue and discarding the undated ones client-side.

get.summary: Answers across every project in the org.
get.description:
Answers across every project in the org.

The org comes from the validated principal and never from the request: a
caller able to name the org could read another tenant's backlog, and a search
is exactly the shape that would quietly return it.

parameters.name: q
parameters.description:
Q matches an issue's title or description. A word from the issue, which is
what someone remembers — not its number, which is what they are looking up.

parameters.name: project
parameters.description:
Project narrows to one team key; "" searches every project in the org,
which is the point of this op.

parameters.name: status
parameters.description: Status keeps one board column: backlog, todo, in_progress, done, canceled.

parameters.name: kind
parameters.description: Kind keeps one shape: issue, pr, epic.

parameters.name: repo
parameters.description: Repo keeps issues bound to one git repository.

parameters.name: source
parameters.description:
Source keeps one origin: team, git, crm, helpdesk, cms, agent. "git" is
how you ask for the mirrored GitHub issues specifically.

parameters.name: assignee
parameters.description: Assignee keeps issues held by one person. Pass "me" for yourself.

parameters.name: limit
parameters.description:
Limit caps the answer; 0 means the default, and anything above the ceiling
is clamped rather than refused — a search that errors on being too broad
teaches people to guess.

get.summary: Returns the boards of your org — the places your work actually is.
get.description:
Returns the boards of your org — the places your work actually
is. The key addresses the board's issues.

A BOARD IS A PLACE WORK IS, not an object somebody provisioned. So the list is
assembled from the work itself: the repositories your org has filed issues on,
plus the boards the index holds. A repository with nothing on it is not in the
list and is still perfectly addressable — GET /projects/<name> reads it and a
create files into it — so nothing is lost by leaving it out.

Measured, which is why: reading the forge's whole repository inventory put 745
boards here, of which all but a handful were vendored forks and mirrors
(.github, .profile, DOMPurify, BoatAttack) that will never carry this org's
work. A list that long is not a list — the estate's real roadmap was in it
somewhere and no one could see it.

The forge half is the FORGE's answer for your own account, so two people in
one org can legitimately see different boards.

post.summary: Refused — a board is a repository on the forge
post.description:
Answers 405. A todo board IS a repository on this deployment's forge, so creating, renaming and deleting one is a FORGE operation carried out with FORGE permissions.

Offering it here would put a second door on the same object, guarded by this surface instead of by the forge — a weaker guard on the same thing. So the route exists and refuses, rather than 404ing: "not this service's job" and "no such thing" are different facts, and the body names the forge so a caller knows where the job IS done.

What this surface DOES own is the work on a board: list the boards you can see, read and file their issues, move a card between columns, and read the schedule a milestone is. Those are the routes beside this one.

get.summary: Returns one board of your org by its key — the repository name.
get.description:
Returns one board of your org by its key — the repository name.
404 when your org has no repository under that key, or when your own forge
account cannot see it.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description:
Key is the project's org-unique handle: 2-8 uppercase alphanumerics starting
with a letter ("ENG", "OPS2"). Matched case-insensitively.

post.summary: Opens a work item on the board — an issue on that repository on the deployment's forge, filed as YOU.
post.description:
Opens a work item on the board — an issue on that repository on
the deployment's forge, filed as YOU.

The column and priority are written as LABELS, which is what makes the card
and the forge issue the same object: someone relabelling in the forge web UI
has moved your card.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key is the board — the repository name, from the path.

get.summary: Returns ONE work item in full — its description included.
get.description:
Returns ONE work item in full — its description included.

The list reads answer a board, and a board is a summary: the description is
where the actual content of a work item lives — what an issue asks for, what
an epic's acceptance criteria are — and no read on this surface returned it.
The address is the one PATCH already accepts, so an item you can move is now
an item you can read.

It reads the forge directly rather than filtering the org fan-out, then falls
back to the index for a board the forge has never heard of — the same order,
and the same reason, as GetProject: a row is one kind of thing however it came
to exist, so a caller does not have to know which store it is in to fetch it.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key is the board — the repository name, or an index board's key.

parameters.name: num
parameters.description: Num is the issue's number on that board.

patch.summary: Edits a work item — rename it, rewrite it, move it to another column, or re-prioritise it.
patch.description:
Edits a work item — rename it, rewrite it, move it to another
column, or re-prioritise it. Absent fields are left alone.

MOVING A CARD IS A RELABEL. The column lives in the forge's label set, so the
move replaces that set rather than writing a status column here that a
forge-side change could contradict. Moving to `done` also CLOSES the issue on
the forge, because a done card and an open issue are a contradiction.

parameters.name: key
parameters.description: Key is the board — the repository name, from the path.

parameters.name: num
parameters.description: Num is the issue number on that repository, from the path.

post.summary: Takes an issue: it becomes yours and it moves to in_progress.
post.description:
Takes an issue: it becomes yours and it moves to in_progress.

The holder is the CALLER, never an argument. "Assign this to someone else" is
a different act with different authority, and it already exists as a PATCH;
conflating them would let anyone hand work to anyone by naming them.

Claiming something already held by someone else is refused rather than
silently taken — two agents on one issue is the failure this prevents, and a
claim that quietly wins a race is worse than one that says no.

key.description: Key is the board — the repository name, from the path.

num.description: Num is the issue number on that repository, from the path.

status.description: Status moves the card to another column.

dueAt.description: unix seconds; absent = no due date

source.description: team | git | crm | helpdesk | cms | agent

key.description: Key is the board — the repository name, from the path.

priority.description: Priority is one of none, urgent, high, medium or low.

status.description:
Status is the board column to open into: backlog, todo, in_progress, done
or canceled. Empty opens into backlog.

bearer.description: The caller's credential, sent as `Authorization: Bearer <token>`. It is either an access token minted by Hanzo IAM or an API key (pk-/sk-). X-Authorization, and HTTP Basic carrying the token as the password, are accepted spellings of the same header for clients that cannot set Authorization; a browser presents the session cookie instead. Every operation requires it unless it says `security: []`.
